evidence.title: Recent Advances in Non-Destructive Testing Technology for Coated Steel Structure Welds.
evidence.abstract: The fabrication of a steel structure facility in the aerospace sector was executed through the implementation of welding techniques. In order to reduce the effects of environmental corrosion and extend its service life, it is typically coated with a protective layer. Nevertheless, conventional non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques generally necessitate preliminary procedures, such as coating removal and surface grinding, prior to inspection, leading to elevated costs and diminished efficiency. Consequently, the investigation into NDT methodologies for welds encased under coatings is of considerable practical significance. The objective of this paper is to comprehensively review and thoroughly analyze the latest research progress in NDT techniques for detecting defects in coated steel welds, seeking feasible approaches for achieving NDT on coated steel structures. Firstly, the paper examines the hazards of common weld defects and the challenges coatings pose to NDT operations. The text then proceeds to expound upon the principles, research advancements, and application scenarios of multiple NDT methods currently available for detecting defects beneath coatings. A comparative summary of these methods is provided, focusing on detection capabilities, coating penetration abilities, key advantages, and limitations. In conclusion, the paper provides insights into future development trends.

evidence.title: Recent Progress of Liquid Metal-Based Electromagnetic Shielding Materials.
evidence.abstract: Electromagnetic shielding materials are pivotal for suppressing electromagnetic radiation and mitigating potential health risks that electronic devices may pose to humans. Beyond health protection, they also hold significant strategic value in safeguarding national information security and maintaining stability. In the research of electromagnetic shielding materials, continuous technological advancements and growing application demands have driven the emergence of various novel materials. Among these, liquid metal (LM) exhibits outstanding properties-including exceptional electrical conductivity, excellent fluidity, and superior deformability-which endow it with substantial potential for application in electromagnetic shielding. Looking ahead, with the continuous advancement in related technologies, liquid metal-based electromagnetic shielding materials are expected to provide effective solutions to key challenges such as electromagnetic pollution and interference. This contribution synthesizes the latest literature. First, it clarifies the nomenclature and classification of liquid metals, as well as the fundamental framework for electromagnetic shielding. Then, it systematically distills recent research advances based on four key design motifs. These motifs include monolithic liquid metal (LM) scaffolds, LM/conductive-filler blends, LM/magnetic particle composites, and architectured multifunctional architectures. Finally, this review identifies current bottlenecks in the field and outlines directions for future development, which aim to achieve ultra-lightweight, broadband, and intelligent LM-based electromagnetic shields.

evidence.title: Cryogenic thermal conductivity measurements on candidate materials for space missions.
evidence.abstract: Spacecraft and instruments on space missions are built using a wide variety of carefully-chosen materials. It is common for NASA engineers to propose new candidate materials which have not been totally characterized at cryogenic temperatures. In many cases a material's cryogenic thermal conductivity must be known before selecting it for a specific space-flight application. We developed a test facility in 2004 at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center to measure the longitudinal thermal conductivity of materials at temperatures between 4 and 300 Kelvin, and we have characterized many candidate materials since then. The measurement technique is not extremely complex, but proper care to details of the setup, data acquisition and data reduction is necessary for high precision and accuracy. We describe the thermal conductivity measurement process and present results for ten engineered materials, including alloys, polymers, composites, and a ceramic.

evidence.title: Analytical modelling of thermal residual stresses and optimal design of ZrO2/(ZrO2+Ni) sandwich ceramics
evidence.abstract: The joining of ceramics with metals have been extensively used in applications requiring high strength and excellent heat insulation. However, evaluating the residual stress generated inevitably due to the mismatch in coefficients of thermal expansion of ceramic and metal is challenging, which is very important for fabrication and characterization of layered inhomogeneous material. A simplified analytical model considering the overall deformation compatibility is established to compute the interlaminar residual stresses of the ZrO2/(ZrO2+Ni) sandwich ceramics, which agrees well with the results obtained by the commercial finite element package. The effects of the thickness ratio of the transitional layer to the middle layer, and the number of transitional layers on the properties of the ZrO2/(ZrO2+Ni) sandwich ceramics are researched to obtain the optimal structure.

evidence.title: Leakage analysis of gasketed flange joints under combined internap pressure and thermal loading
evidence.abstract: Leakage in Gasketed Flanged Joints (GFJs) have always been a great problem for the process industry. The sealing performance of a GFJ depends on its installation and applied loading conditions. This paper aims to finding the leak rate through ANSI class#150 flange joints using a compressed asbestos sheet (CAS) gasket under combined structural and thermal transient loading conditions using two different leak rate models and two different bolt-up levels. The first model is a Gasket Compressive Strain model in which strains are determined using finite element analysis. The other model is based on Porous Media Theory in which gasket is considered as porous media. Leakage rates are determined using both leak rate models and are compared against appropriate tightness classes and the effectiveness of each approach is presented

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: The fabrication of a steel structure facility in the aerospace sector was executed through the implementation of welding techniques. In order to reduce the effects of environmental corrosion and extend its service life, it is typically coated with a protective layer. Nevertheless, conventional non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques generally necessitate preliminary procedures, such as coating removal and surface grinding, prior to inspection, leading to elevated costs and diminished efficiency. Consequently, the investigation into NDT methodologies for welds encased under coatings is of considerable practical significance. The objective of this paper is to comprehensively review and thoroughly analyze the latest research progress in NDT techniques for detecting defects in coated steel welds, seeking feasible approaches for achieving NDT on coated steel structures. Firstly, the paper examines the hazards of common weld defects and the challenges coatings pose to NDT operations. The text then proceeds to expound upon the principles, research advancements, and application scenarios of multiple NDT methods currently available for detecting defects beneath coatings. A comparative summary of these methods is provided, focusing on detection capabilities, coating penetration abilities, key advantages, and limitations. In conclusion, the paper provides insights into future development trends.

custody_records.raw_content: Electromagnetic shielding materials are pivotal for suppressing electromagnetic radiation and mitigating potential health risks that electronic devices may pose to humans. Beyond health protection, they also hold significant strategic value in safeguarding national information security and maintaining stability. In the research of electromagnetic shielding materials, continuous technological advancements and growing application demands have driven the emergence of various novel materials. Among these, liquid metal (LM) exhibits outstanding properties-including exceptional electrical conductivity, excellent fluidity, and superior deformability-which endow it with substantial potential for application in electromagnetic shielding. Looking ahead, with the continuous advancement in related technologies, liquid metal-based electromagnetic shielding materials are expected to provide effective solutions to key challenges such as electromagnetic pollution and interference. This contribution synthesizes the latest literature. First, it clarifies the nomenclature and classification of liquid metals, as well as the fundamental framework for electromagnetic shielding. Then, it systematically distills recent research advances based on four key design motifs. These motifs include monolithic liquid metal (LM) scaffolds, LM/conductive-filler blends, LM/magnetic particle composites, and architectured multifunctional architectures. Finally, this review identifies current bottlenecks in the field and outlines directions for future development, which aim to achieve ultra-lightweight, broadband, and intelligent LM-based electromagnetic shields.

custody_records.raw_content: Spacecraft and instruments on space missions are built using a wide variety of carefully-chosen materials. It is common for NASA engineers to propose new candidate materials which have not been totally characterized at cryogenic temperatures. In many cases a material's cryogenic thermal conductivity must be known before selecting it for a specific space-flight application. We developed a test facility in 2004 at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center to measure the longitudinal thermal conductivity of materials at temperatures between 4 and 300 Kelvin, and we have characterized many candidate materials since then. The measurement technique is not extremely complex, but proper care to details of the setup, data acquisition and data reduction is necessary for high precision and accuracy. We describe the thermal conductivity measurement process and present results for ten engineered materials, including alloys, polymers, composites, and a ceramic.

custody_records.raw_content: Leakage in Gasketed Flanged Joints (GFJs) have always been a great problem for the process industry. The sealing performance of a GFJ depends on its installation and applied loading conditions. This paper aims to finding the leak rate through ANSI class#150 flange joints using a compressed asbestos sheet (CAS) gasket under combined structural and thermal transient loading conditions using two different leak rate models and two different bolt-up levels. The first model is a Gasket Compressive Strain model in which strains are determined using finite element analysis. The other model is based on Porous Media Theory in which gasket is considered as porous media. Leakage rates are determined using both leak rate models and are compared against appropriate tightness classes and the effectiveness of each approach is presented
